title: The Completion Accounts Clause: The Reason Your Sale Price Can Still Move After You've Signed
linkedin:
The sale price gets agreed. The contract gets signed. Three months later, a reconciliation clause can still take six figures off what actually lands in your account.

It is called a completion accounts adjustment, and it sits inside most Australian SME sale agreements whether the seller noticed it at signing or not.

Here is how it works. The price assumes the business holds a certain level of working capital, debtors less payables, stock on hand, accrued leave, on the day ownership changes hands. What gets banked at settlement is provisional. The real number gets locked in later, once the buyer's accountants prepare completion accounts and true up the price against that assumed target.

Nobody is doing anything wrong here. It is a standard mechanism built to protect both sides from the gap between the financials used to set the price and the real state of the business on handover day.

The sellers who come out closest to the number they expected are the ones who manage working capital deliberately in the run up to a sale, not just report on it. Debtors chased on normal terms. Stock right sized. Accruals recorded properly, well before anyone is reconciling against them.

The headline multiple is not the full story. What happens to your debtor book and your stock count in the months before completion decides what you actually walk away with.

Ever sold a business and had the final payment land lower than the price you signed for? There is a reason, and it is not anyone being dodgy.

Most sale agreements include a clause that trues up the price against the real working capital position (debtors, stock, accrued leave) on completion day, not the numbers from when you first signed. If your debtor book has crept out or your stock count has gone soft in the lead up to a sale, that gap shows up in the final cheque, months after settlement.

Worth checking your sale agreement for this clause before you are ever in the middle of negotiating one.

If you are a business owner in Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales or Victoria thinking about selling in the next year or two, there is a clause in most sale agreements worth understanding well before you ever get near signing one.

It is called a completion accounts adjustment. The price you agree with a buyer is based on financials from months earlier, but the final figure gets trued up later against the actual working capital, debtors, stock on hand and accrued leave, on the day the sale completes. If that real number comes in under what was assumed, the final payment can be reduced by a meaningful amount, sometimes months after settlement has already happened.

None of this is unusual, and it is not a sign a buyer is trying to catch anyone out. It is standard practice. The owners who protect their number best are the ones who manage their debtor book and stock position properly in the run up to a sale, not just once a buyer is already at the table.

If a sale is somewhere on your horizon, it is worth understanding this clause long before the contract lands in front of you. Read the full piece on the blog.
